newsitem.title: POLAND: Peasant protest no hurdle for 1998 budget - finmin.
newsitem.headline: Peasant protest no hurdle for 1998 budget - finmin.

text.p: Poland's finance minister said on Thursday he will continue to work on the 1998 national budget assuming a slashed deficit despite opposition from the co-ruling Peasant Party (PSL).

The minister, Marek Belka, said that during a cabinet session on Thursday the ministers discussed ways to find additional revenues but no one questioned his plan to cut the deficit to 1.9 percent of gross domestic product next year from the 2.8 percent planned for 1997.
"There was a discussion about possiblities of mobilising additional revenues...but the (1.9 percent) deficit is unchangeable," Belka told Reuters in a brief interview.
He added that Poland's capital market was in any case too shallow to allow the government to finance a higher deficit.

Belka said he would now start working on spending caps for particular ministries, assuming that budget revenues would be 133.3 billion zlotys with spending of 142.9 billion zlotys and a deficit of 9.6 billion zlotys.

The budget would be constructed under the assumptions that GDP next year would continue to grow at 5.5 percent annually and that inflation would fall to 9.5 percent year-on-year in December 1998 from 14.6 percent in May.

Belka's budgetary plans were questioned on Wednesday by the Peasants, the smaller party in the governing coalition, on grounds that they would hit farmers' income, curb investment and boost unemployment.

The party instructed its cabinet members to vote against the finance ministry's plans but Belka said that Prime Minister Wlodzimierz Cimoszewicz decided there would be no cabinet vote on the proposals on Thursday.
The cabinet vote on the budget, when its full draft is ready, will most likely be in early September, Belka said.
The ruling coalition's stronger party, the ex-communist Democratic Left Alliance (SLD), has so far supported Belka's plans and can outvote the Peasants at government sessions.
Belka dismissed the Peasants' objections as electioneering before the September 21 parliamentary polls.
"We would like to submit the budget to the next parliament at its first session along with the resignation of the prime minister," he said.
The finance minister has said the deficit must be radically lowered to stifle domestic demand and put the widening trade gap under control.

The central bank says that if the current account deficit, forecast to grow to $6 billion this year from $1.35 billion in 1996, expands too much in 1998 Poland might eventually have to devalue the zloty. It says this would boost inflation and undermine economic growth.
The bank, the National Bank of Poland (NBP), has suggested that a balanced 1998 budget would be the best measure to avoid the kind of financial crisis recently experienced by the Czech Republic.
The Czech Republic had to devalue its currency and take strict anti-import measures after its foreign trade deficit ballooned and industrial output shrank.
But Belka said a balanced budget was impossible in 1998.

"Of course, from the monetary policy point of view, it would be better to have an even tighter budget, but one also has to take into consideration other facts, not only social and political but also economic," he said.
National Bank of Poland head Hanna Gronkiewicz-Waltz said in a newspaper on Thursday that a 1.9 percent deficit would make it more likely that an interest rate rise would be necessary to cool demand.
She added Poland could afford a 1.5 percent deficit next year if it led to a balanced budget in 1999.
"I would think with dread about the possibility of increased rates," Belka commented, without elaborating. -- Warsaw Newsroom +48 22 653 9700
